title: Christ, first in God's plan
hook: Franciscan thinkers held Christ would have come even without sin; others disagree

segments.voice: Yesterday, Duns Scotus and his strange word, haecceity: thisness. Your line was this one. Who did you catch yourself treating as a type, and what did you see when you looked again? Day one thousand two hundred twenty.

Here's a question with no way to check the answer. Suppose Adam and Eve had never sinned. Suppose the whole human story had gone right from the start. Would there still have been a Christmas? Would the Son of God still have been born in Bethlehem? It sounds like a question for a sleepless night, not a classroom. But medieval teachers took it seriously, because the answer says something about why Christ came at all. Was he God's rescue plan, sent because things went wrong? Or was he the plan from the beginning? Today, two honest answers, and the friar who gave the second one.
screen: `WHAT IF NO ONE HAD SINNED?` → `WOULD THERE STILL BE CHRISTMAS?` → `RESCUE, OR THE PLAN?`

segments.voice: Start with Thomas Aquinas. He looks at scripture and notices that whenever it gives a reason for the Son of God becoming man, the reason is sin: he came to save. So, Aquinas says, it's more fitting to say that if humanity had not sinned, the Incarnation would not have happened. And he adds a careful line: God's power isn't limited by that. God could have done it anyway. The Church sings something close to this view at the Easter Vigil, in a hymn that calls Adam's sin a happy fault, because it won so great a Redeemer. Now Duns Scotus, the Franciscan, from yesterday. He comes at it from love, not from the problem. God, he says, does things in order. When you plan a house, you think of the house first and the bricks after. God's first and highest intention, the thing all of creation is for, is Christ: the Son joined to a human nature, the masterpiece of God's love. Everything else is willed for his sake. So Christ wasn't a patch for a broken plan. He was the plan. Sin changed the way he came, as a Redeemer who suffered. But he would have come. Scotus leans on Saint Paul's letter to the Colossians, which says of Christ, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For in him were all things created." Firstborn of every creature. Franciscan thinkers after Scotus took this up as their own. Both answers are held by Catholics, and the Church hasn't chosen between them. One sees Christ as the rescuer who came because we fell. The other sees him as the reason there was a world to fall in.
screen: `AQUINAS: HE CAME BECAUSE OF SIN.` · `O HAPPY FAULT.` · `SCOTUS: CHRIST WAS WILLED FIRST.` · `BOTH ANSWERS HELD; NONE CHOSEN.` · then, large: `THE FIRSTBORN OF EVERY CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wonder about God's plan. Settle, and breathe. This isn't a puzzle to solve in two minutes. Just hold the two pictures side by side. In one, the world goes wrong and Christ comes to set it right. In the other, the world was made with Christ in mind from the start, and he would have come anyway. Notice which one your mind leans toward, and which one is harder to picture. Then let both rest. If you pray, you can simply thank God for Christ, however the plan was drawn. If you don't, just stay with the question and the breath, without needing an answer. The bell holds the time.
Christ. For Scotus and those who followed him, not God's backup plan but the first thing God willed, the firstborn of every creature. Today's word.
Your line: christ first. Today, look at one thing that went wrong and ask whether the good in your life was only ever a repair, or there from the start. Day one thousand two hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Catholics are free to hold either view on why the Son of God became man; theologians in the line of Scotus teach the primacy of Christ, and theologians in the line of Aquinas teach that the Incarnation was willed as the remedy for sin.

myth: the Church has settled the question and ruled Scotus wrong
both answers are held by Catholics, and the Church hasn't chosen between them.
Aquinas said God could not have become man without sin
he said it was more fitting to say so, but that God's power isn't limited by it.
Scotus thought sin changed the way Christ came, but not whether he came
for Scotus, Christ was willed first; sin made him come as a suffering Redeemer.

fork.setup: you're Duns Scotus. someone asks whether the Son of God would have become man if no one had ever sinned. what do you answer?
options: no; he came only to fix what went wrong.
yes; Christ was God's first intention, sin or no sin.
no one can say anything about it.
fork.reveal: Scotus says Christ was willed first, the masterpiece of God's love. Aquinas leaned the other way, and the Church allows both.

original.note: Greek: the anointed one, the New Testament's word for the Hebrew Messiah.

trapdoor: what you thought: Christ came because the world went wrong.
what it means: one Catholic answer says so; the Franciscan answer says he was God's plan from the start.
what a scholar hears: the medieval debate on the motive of the Incarnation, Aquinas in the Summa against Scotus on the primacy of Christ.

sources.quoted: Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For in him were all things created.

sources.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae III, q. 1, a. 3
John Duns Scotus, Ordinatio III, d. 7, q. 3

notes: Aquinas (ST III q.1 a.3) paraphrased: scripture everywhere assigns sin as the reason, so it is more fitting to say the Incarnation would not have occurred without sin, though God's power is not limited. Confirm.

Scotus (Ordinatio III d.7 q.3; also Reportatio) paraphrased: an orderly willer wills the end first; Christ's glory willed first, not occasioned by sin. The house/bricks image is the script's own illustration, not Scotus's words; confirm acceptable.
'The Church hasn't chosen between them' / 'Catholics are free to hold either view': confirm this is accurate to say.
Exsultet 'O felix culpa' paraphrased ('happy fault ... so great a Redeemer'), not quoted; confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Colossians 1:15–16 (quoted to 'all things created').
Editor pass: the word line's 'Scotus and the Franciscans after him' (implying all Franciscans) changed to 'Scotus and those who followed him'.
